Medical Facilities for the Poor at AllMS 
† *363. SHRI D. P. YADAV:  Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that due to lack of medical equipments and shortage of beds 
in All India Institute of Medical Sciences, the people coming from rural areas have to 
face lot of hardships and have to stay in lawns and verandahs; 
(b) whether the Institute has become a hospital for the rich and VIPs only; if so, the 
reasons therefor; and 
(c) whether Government are going to  take any initiatives to provide 
better medical facilities to the people coming from rural and remote areas? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
(a) to (c) The Institute's hospital (including Centres) has 1626 beds and it is well 
equipped within the financial resources available. Adequate medical care is provided 
to all the patients who come for treatment irrespective of their social and economic 
status. 
To cater to the needs of poor people coming from far flung areas, the Institute 
has the Rajgarhia Vishram Sadan for providing accommodation with adequate facilities 
to about 250 persons at a time. In tune with the Institute's basic mandate of 
responsiveness to the needs of the genuinely poor, all services are provided free of cost 
to the poor and the needy, except OPD Registration Charges.

† *373. SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH: SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be please to state: 
 whether it is a fact that ample possibi lities exist to earn financial benefits

products;

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) The National Forest Policy, 1988 provides the basic principles 
for management of forests. According to th e policy, the principal aim of the forest 
management is to ensure environmental stability and maintenance of ecological 
balance. The derivation of direct economic benefit is subordinate to the principal aim. 
The protection, improvement and enhancement of production of Minor Forest 
Produce with due regard to generation of employment and income has been identified 
as one of the essentials of forest manageme nt. The policy also stresses for sufficient 
provision of fodder, fuel and pasture, specifically in areas adjoining forest, in order to 
prevent depletion of forest beyond the sustainable limit. The Policy envisages for 
intensive afforestation programme with special emphasis on augmenting fuel wood 
production to meet requirement of the rural people. 
The Ministry of Environment and Forests is implementing various certrally 
sponsored afforestation schemes in conformity with above principals. For sustainbale 
development and conservation of forest, a long term perspective plan "National Forestry 
Action Programme' has been prepared. 
(c) and (d) It has been decided to involve village communities and Non-
governmental Organisations in the regeneration, management and protection of forests 
through Joint Forest Management. Twenty-two states have so far adopted and programme 
and at present about 10.248 million hectares of forests are managed through 36,130 Joint 
Forests Management Committees in various States.

 whether it is a fact that Government have wasted crores of rupees to save the river 
Ganges from pollution, as reported in Pioneer dated 22nd July, 2000;

 whether Ganga Action Plan has totally failed to save the river Ganges;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) to (c) No, Sir. Goverment of India has spent Rs. 451.70 
crores on pollution abatement works under Ganga Action Plan Phase I which has been 
declared closed since 31.3.2000. With the completion of these works, it has been 
possible to minimise the organic pollution reaching the Ganga river wherever the works 
have been made operational. However, there has been only an incidental reduction in die 
level of microbial pollution in the treated sewage reaching the river. This is due to the fact 
mat technologies for reducing microbial pollution are either cost intensive or need large 
areas of land. Moreover, under Ganga Action Plan Phase I, only about 35 per cent of die 
pollution load presently being generated from all die towns along me river has been tackled. 
The remaining pollution load is to be tackled under Ganga Action Plan Phase II which is 
under implementation. The Ganga Action Plan Phase II covers pollution abatement works on 
Ganga and its major tributories viz. Yamuna, Gomati and Damodar. As a result die impact of 
the first phase works of the Ganga Action Plan on river water quality is not adequately 
visible. 
(d) and (e) Government is not aware of die proceedings of die World Water 
Commission. However, Ganga is a polluted river as only about 35 percent of its pollution has 
been tackled under the Ganga Action Plan Phase I. The following remedial steps have been 
taken by die Government under the Ganga Action Plan Phase II. 
(i) State Governments have been asked to take advance action for land 
acquisition wherever applicable after which only die related schemes be 
approved. Release of Central grants and its utilisation by die State 
Governments is monitored more vigorously to minimise instances of 
diversion of funds. 
(ii) Release of Central grants under die second phase of Ganga Action Plan to Bihar 
was widheld for some time till a firm commitment from die State Government 
was available for providing adequate

funds for operation and maintenance of the assets. The matter is also being 
pursued with the State Government of UP for adequate provision of 
funds for operation and maintenance of assets. Operation and maintenance of 
assets in West Bengal is generally satisfactory. 
(iii) The State Governments have been asked to ensure continuous supply 
of electricity for assets through dedicated feeders wherever required. 
(iv) To address the problem of microbial pollution, it has been decided to 
adopt land based technologies for sewage treatment wherever feasible 
or to use conventional technologies of sewage disinfection.

(c) Steps taken for containment of Malaria include:— 
 Intensification of early detection and prompt treatment of Malaria 
including treatment of complicated cases by newer drugs. 
 Intensification of vector control measures through prioritization of areas 
for selective spray with appropriate insecticides and alternative and 
integrated vector control methods. 
 Introduction of newer insecticides like Synthetic Pyrethroids for selective 
use as per technical requirements. 
 Intensification of Information Education and Communication (IEC) 
activities for public awareness and community participation. 
 Institutional and management capacity building, manpower development 
through intensive re-orientation training programmes at all levels and 
efficient Management Information System (MIS). 
 Implementation of an enhanced Malaria Control Project (EMCP) with 
World Bank support under the National Anti Malaria Programme 
(NAMP) since September, 1997, covering 1045 primary Health Centres 
(PHCs) in 100 predominantly tribal highly Malaria-endemic districts of 7 
peninsular States, namely, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Orissa, Gujarat, 
Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan and 19 cities/towns having 
high endemicity of malaria in these States and the States of Karnataka, 
Tamil Nadu and West Bengal, for intensification of Malaria Control 
activities by way of additional inputs through a mix of interventions. 
 Providing 100% Central assistance to (he 7 North Eastern States since 
December, 1994 under NMEP.

Haryana and Punjab becoming drought prone 
2809. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that according to a recent report from 
environmentalists, Haryana and Punjab are heading towards becoming the 
country's least productive and drought prone areas; 
 whether erosion, salinity, inappropriate cropping pattern, deforestation, urban 
sprawl and over-exploitation of natural resources are now posing a threat to the green 
revolution; and 
 if so, what is Government's reaction in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI): (a) to (c) In Haryana and Punjab, due to intensive 
cropping, there is more mining of micro and macro nutrients and withdrawal of 
excessive water leading to declining productivity. Although the growth rate of 
productivity has declined in Punjab recently, the productivity per hectare has not 
declined. The present wheat yield in Punjab still compares favourably with many 
countries in the world. The falling of water table relates specifically to sweet water zone 
due to early transplantation of rice. However, there is no report of drought in Haryana 
and Punjab. The problem of secondary salinisation particularly in canal irrigated areas is 
increasing due to more seepage. 
60 

[ 18 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Proper lining of canals and judicious use of water are being advocated to mitigate this 
problem. In order to check soil erosion, bio-engineering measures have been suggested. 
Integrated use of natural resources and introduction of legumes in cropping system are 
also being popularised to sustain higher productivity. Under the National Watershed 
Development Programme of the Ministry of Agriculture, which, inter alia, includes 
enhancement of agricultural productivity in a sustainable manner, an area of 35,520 ha. 
in Haryana and 19,792 ha. in Punjab has been treated so far.

2841. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of

 whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item, "AIDS 
is the biggest killer in India: UN", publis hed in the Asian Age dated the 23rd July,

 whether Government have any proposal to tackle this menace with a

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. While the estimates of HIV 
infections are on the basis of surveillance reports undertaken annually by Government, the number 
of deaths quoted in the report are mere projections. Government, therefore, does not agree with the 
UNAIDS report. 
(c) and (d) In order to prevent and contro l the spread of HIV/AIDS in India, a 
comprehensive Programme is currently under implementation throughout the country as a 
Centrally sponsored scheme. The project is being implemented with the assistance from World 
Bank, United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and Department for 
International Development (DFID) of U.K. The main components consist of:— 
 Reducing the spread of HIV in groups at high risk by identification of target populations 
and providing peer counselling, condom promotion, treatment of sexually 
transmitted infections. 
 Preventive intervention for the general population by Information, Education and 
Communication (IEC) and awareness campaign, provision of voluntary testing and 
counselling, safe blood transfusion services and prevention of occupational exposure. 
 Providing financial assistance for opportunistic infections, home and community 
based care to people living with HIV/AIDS. 
 Strengthening effectiveness and technical managerial, financial sustainabiiity at 
National, State and Municipal levels. 
 Promoting collaboration amongst public, private and voluntary sectors.

FAMILY WELFARE (DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) While the estimates of HIV infections are on the basis of surveillance 
reports undertaken annually by Government, the number of deaths quoted in the report 
are mere projections. Government, therefore, does not agree with the UNAIDS report 
on number of deaths. For the control of the disease, Government has taken the 
following steps: 
(i) Reducing the spread of HIV in groups at high risk by identification of 
target populations and providing peer counselling, condom promotion, 
treatment of sexually transmitted infections. 
(ii) Preventive intervention for the general population by Information, 
Education and Communication (IEC) and awareness campaign, 
provision of voluntary testing and counselling, safe blood transfusion 
services and prevention of occupational exposure. 
(iii) Providing financial assistance fo r opportunistic infections, home and 
community based care to people l i v i n g  with HIV/ AIDS. 
(iv) Strengthening effectiveness an d technical, managerial, financial 
sustainability at National, State and Municipal levels. 
(v) Promoting collaboration amongst public, private and voluntary sectors. 
(d) and (e) Even though the sentinel surveillance data of 1998 and 1999 reveals 
that there is no increase in HIV prevalence rates in the State of Tamil Nadu, it cannot be 
concluded without further observation that Tamil Nadu has succeeded in controlling 
AIDS. Based on Tamil Nadu State AIDS Control Society Model, the programme is 
being implemented in other States for expediting flow of funds and implementation of 
programme components.

Panel to Review the Population Policy 
2854. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state; 
(a) whether Government have set up a panel to control population in the 
country; if so the details thereof; 
(b) whether Government have also prepared any action plan to 
operationalise the National Population Policy; if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the steps taken by Government and family welfare devices and services 
all over the country; 
 whether Government propose to set up a separate department of Population 
Control; and 
 if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA): (a) As envisaged in the 
National Population Policy, 2000 a National Commission on Population has been 
constituted on 11th May, 2000 under the Chairmanship of Prime Minister to oversee 
and review the implementation of the Policy. 
(b) The National Population Policy, 2000 enumerates Action Plan for each of 
the strategic themes envisaged for achieving population stabilisation in the country. 
These operational strategies are listed below: 
 Decentralised planning and programme implementation. 
 Convergence of service delivery at village levels. 
 Empowering women for improved health and nutrition. 
 Child survival and child health 
 Meeting the unmet needs for family welfare services. 
 Under-served population groups: 
Urban slums; 
Tribal communities, hill area population and displaced and 
migrant populations; 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [ 18 A ugust, 2000] 
Adolescents; 
Increased participation of men in planned parenthood. 
 Diverse health care provides. 
 Collaboration with and commitments from non-government 
organisations and the private sector. 
 Mainstream Indian Systems of Medicine and Homeopathy. 
 
 Contraceptive technology and research on reproductive and child 
health. 
 Providing for the older population. 
 Information, Education and Communication 
(c) The following steps are being taken under the National Family Welfare 
Programme to stabilize the increase in populate; 
(i) An integrated and holistic programme of Reproductive and Child Health 
that include Maternal health, Child Health and Contraception issues was 
launched since, 1997. 
(ii)  Information, Education and Communication Programme to create 
awareness about the benefits of small family. 
(iii)  Assistance to State / UTs to maintain certain family welfare 
infrastructure. 
(iv)  Assistance to Voluntary Organizations and NGOs for implementing family 
welfare programme. 
The National Population Policy has been approved by the Government in 
February, 2000. The Policy seeks to put in place a multi sectoral agenda for population 
stabilisation which includes increasing out-reach and coverage of reproductive and 
child health care services, strengthening of health infrastructure, meeting the unmet 
needs for contraception services, and converging of integrated service delivery at 
village and house hold levels. 
(d) and (e) There is already a separate Department, viz. the Department of 
Family Welfare within Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to monitor the 
National Family Welfare Programme.

RAJYA SABHA [ 18 August, 2000] 
(d) if so, the steps taken to set up primary schools, out of Central grants, in those 
revenue villages in Orissa? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) The main responsibility for setting up of primary schools 
rests with the State Government/Union Territory Administration concerned. The 
Central Government only supplements their efforts in this direction through Centrally 
sponsored schemes/programmes. 
(b) Government of Orissa have a policy of opening Primary Schools in 
unserved revenue villages which meet the following twin norms of distance 
and population:— 
(i) A village with 300 population in plain area. 
(ii) A village with 200 population in hilly/tribal area. 
(iii) There should not be any schooling facility within one kilometre radius of 
the village. 
The Government of Orissa have recently decided in principle to launch the 
Education Guarantee Scheme (EGS). 
 As per the 6th All India Educational Survey, out of a total of 31667 
habitations predominantly populated by STs in Orissa, 23226 habitations have a 
primary school within or upto one kilometre of the habitation. Out of 7676 habitations 
predominantly populated by SCs, 6467 habitations have a primary school within or upto 
one kilometre of the habitation. 
 A major Centrally sponsored programme namely District Primary Education 
Programme (DPEP) is presently being implemented in 8 districts of Orissa and coverage 
of another 8 districts of the State under the above programme is in the pipeline. In the 
existing 8 DPEP districts, 734 new primary schools have been opened and another 689 
primary schools are proposed to be opened in the 8 expansion districts in tribal and SC 
dominated habitations. 
380 Alternative Schools have been opened during 1999-2000 and 600 are 
planned to be opened during 2000-2001 in unserved SC/ST dominated habitations 
which do not qualify to have formal Primary Schools as per State Government norm. 
1295 Alternative Schools are proposed to be opened in 8 expansion Districts of 
DPEP in unserved remote SC/ST dominated habitations.

Railway revenues from passenger and freight services 
2907. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that the passenger services account for 59 percent of the 
rail traffic but contribute only 30 per cent of the revenues, while the freight services 
constitute 41 per cent thereof but generate 70 per cent of the total Railway income; 
 if so, the reasons for this lop sides generation; and 
 whether the Planning Commission, in its mid-term appraisal has called upon the 
Railways to correct this imbalance; if so, the action proposed in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. As per the revised estimates for the year 1999-2000 
passenger services accounted for nearly 59 percent of the rail traffic and contributed to 
approximately 29 percent of the revenue. The freight services constituting about 41 
percent of the rail traffic generated approximately 71 percent of the total revenue. 
 The reason for the differential in generation of revenue from passenger and 
freight services is that the Railways have been following a policy of restraint in increasing 
passenger fares as part of their public service obligations. This has caused internal 
cross subsidisation of passenger fares from freight traffic earnings. 
 The Mid-Term Review is still unde r finalisation with the Planning 
Commission.

(b) Accrual of vacancies and filling of the same are continuous processes. 
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Indira Sawhney Vs. Union of India 
held that the number of vacancies to be filled up on the basis of reservation in a year 
including carried-forward reservations should in no case exceed the limit of 50%. As 
per the existing recruitment rules, the to tal reservation for Scheduled Castes / 
Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes in itself is 49.5%. As such, after 1996, 
no further Special Recruitment Drive could be undertaken to wipe out the carried-
forward shortfall vacancies of SCs / STs / OBCs. 
To overcome this difficulty, die Government have passed Constitution (Eighty 
First Amendment) Act 2000, following which necessary instructions have also been 
received from the Department of Personnel and Training (DOP&T) vide their Office 
Memorandum dated 20.7.2000. This Act lays down that the ceiling of 50% on filling up 
of reserved vacancies would apply only on the reserved vacancies which arise in the 
current year and the backlog / carried-forward vacancies would be treated as a separate 
block and would not be subject to any ceiling. Accordingly, vide Railway Board's letter 
dated 4.8.2000, all the Zonal Railways / Production Units etc. have been advised to 
undertake the review of backlog / carried-forward vacancies of SCs / STs and to take 
steps to clear the same. As announced in the Budget 2000-2001, special drive for filling 
in the backlog of SC / ST vacancies are being taken up.

2941. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND

218 

[ 18 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
 whether Government propose to conduct initial trials on genetically

countries, before beginning such cultivation in the country;

 by when these crops are likely to be introduced in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI 
SINGH RAWAT): (a) and (b): Yes, Sir, to assess the environmental safety, taking also 
into account safety to human and animal health. Government is permitting the conduct 
of trials under the Indian Environment (Pro tection) Act, 1986. Genetically Modified 
Crops of cotton, tobacco, tomato, brinjal, cauliflower, cabbage, mustard and potato are 
being tested in Indian environment. 
(c) and (d) Yes Sir, information on many crops is available. Any trial in Indian 
environment requires the assessment of the risks from the available information. No 
open field trial is authorized before the information is evaluated, and the materials are 
tested in laboratory and contained Green House conditions for generating additional 
safety information. 
(e) Only after the Government is satisfied about the biosafety and agronomic 
advantage of genetically modified (G.M) crops, such crops can be permitted to be 
introduced. No GM crop has yet been commericially introduced in the country.

Re. QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU (West Bengal): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would like to 
draw your attention and that of the House to a very serious violation of privilege of 
this House. The Constitution provides that national policies, which are adopted by the 
Government, are subsequently placed on the Table of the House and if there is no 
disapproval motion on that policy document, it is deemed that that policy document is 
the approved policy of 
234 

[18 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Parliament. The National Te lecom Policy was finalised by the Government on 26 th 
March, 1999. Subsequently, since the House was not in Session, the Government was 
kind enough to send the copies of these documents to the Members personally and it 
was accepted, subsequently, that the Policy was deemed to have been placed on the 
Table of the House. Subsequently, there was no disapproval motion. Right now, we 
have one single National Telecom Policy, 1999. Sir, para 3.5 of this Policy, which 
deals with National Long Distance Operator, says, 'National long-distance service 
beyond service area to the private operators will be opened for competition with effect 
from January 1, 2000. To promote setting up longdistance bandwidth capacity in the 
country, provide a choice to consumers and promote competition, all NLDOs should 
be able to access subscribers. With a view  to achieve the above, all access providers 
shall be mandatorily required to provide interconnection to the NLDOs resulting in 
choice for subscribers to make long-distanc e calls through any operator." Now, Sir, it 
is very clear that the intra-circle STD within the service area, that is, the telecom 
circle, is reserved for the fixed service provid ers, which in this case, may either be the 
present DTS or the private licensee, whosoever may be having the licence for that 
particular service area. But, Sir, on the 13 th of this month, th e hon. Communications 
Minister had announced new guidelines for opening up of the national long-distance 
operators. It has been said and I am quoting this from the Economic Times, dated 14th 
August, 2000 : "The policy will permit the national long-distance operators to carry 
intra-circle STD calls, as had been decided at a recent Telecom Commission meeting" 
And, Sir, it is also reported that the earlier Telecom Commission, in keeping with the 
National Telecom Policy, decided that intra- circle STD will be only reserved for the 
fixed service providers. Now, this is a departure from the earlier policy. We have read 
press reports that inbetween the Telecom Commission meetings, a lot of water has 
flown. There was a lot of pressure brought on the Government. Even to this extent that 
the Minister of State for Communications had written a letter to the Prime Minister — 
and that was leaked to the press - which simply abused the Minister of 
Communications and the Telecom Commission for not accepting the pressure tactics 
of the potential national long-distance operators. But, Sir, the more serious thing here 
is this. When there is an approved National Telecom Policy, which is deemed to be 
the policy of Parliament, a departure from that has been made; and that too, when the 
session is going on; that too outside the House. This is a grave infringement on the 
privilege and the prerogatives of the House.    I would, 
235 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2000] 
therefore, Sir, humbly request you, and through you, the entire House that it is a 
question of defending and safeguarding the honour, the prestige, the prerogatives and 
the privileges of this august institution. An d, Sir, I would request you to direct the 
Government not to go ahead with this issue because there is a privilege involved and 
unless the whole matter is resolved, the Government should not issue any notification 
to bring into effect the departure that has taken place from the approved policy. 
MR. CHAIRMAN:  That's all right.

you for giving me an opportunity to raise the matter of fixation of royalty .on lignite.

tonne with effect from 1 st August, 1991, while for lignite, it remained at Rs.2.50 per

Rs.50 per tonne with effect from 11th Octo ber, 1994. Revision of royalty for major 
minerals has to be effected once in three years. The next revision was due from I997.

Nadu Government for refixing of royalty on lignite on par with Grade V coal (F&G). 
the Government of India constituted a study group to examine the question of revision 
of royalty on lignite. The State Government reiterated its view for treating lignite oh 
par with the Grade V coal F&G, as had been  accepted by the Ministry of Energy in 
I990 itself. The Central Fuel Research Institute had confirmed that lignite in Tamil 
Nadu has to be grouped with F-grade coal. The outcome is not known. The matter 
was taken up by the hon. Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu with the hon. Prime Minister, 
as far back as in July, I999. The Governme nt of Tamil Nadu was given to understand 
that it has been agreed to enhance the rate and that it is pending for approval of the 
Cabinet. The Tamil Nadu Government is facing a huge loss of revenue due to 
payment of low royalty on lignite. We request an early approval of the Cabinet and

SHRI B.P. SINGHAL (Uttar Pradesh): Sir, I would like to draw the attention

mystery. All the major bridge s, namely, Songom, Dite Dime and Nubo as well as

Safety of Air Travel 
SHRI R.P. GOENKA (Rajasthan): Sir, I am grateful to you for giving me 
an opportunity to speak on "Safety of Air Travel". 
251 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2000] 
A major air disaster was averted with the chance detection of a six-foot long 
crack on the left wing of an Indian Airlines Airbus 300, bound for Delhi from 
Calcutta, on Saturday morning, the 12 th August, 2000. This aircraft had arrived from 
Delhi on 11 th evening, and had been thoroughly checked by the engineers on night 
duty and cleared for take-off. It was only by chance that the engineers at the departure 
noticed the crack when the luggage had been loaded on flight IC 264 and the 
passengers were about to board the aircraft. Apparently, there is a dereliction of duty 
and negligence on the part of the staff to leave a visible crack on the wing of the 
aircraft unchecked, or, perhaps, the old age of the aircraft. This is not an isolated 
incident. On many other earlier occasions also, similar negligence on the part of the 
staff had been noticed. The recent accidents which have taken place have been, to a 
large extent, caused by ill-maintained aircraft and inadequate and improper 
maintenance of the facilities at the airport. These incidents have created apprehensions 
among the travelling public about the safety of  Indian Airlines aircraft. It is also for 
this reason that in spite of inconvenience, pa ssengers prefer to travel by other airlines. 
I want to know from the Minister of Civil Aviation the steps taken for improving the 
system to ensure complete safety of aircraft and replacing the aircraft, and the penal 
action taken against the defaulting staff.

SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI (Kerala): Mr. Chairman, Sir, 
Parliament passed the National Commission for Safai Karamcharis Act, 1993 and a 
National Commission for Safai Karamcharis was constituted thereunder in August, 
1994 with the objective to promote and safeguard the interests and rights of Safai 
Karamcharis.

1997 and in April 1997, Parliament through an amendment extended the validity of 
the Safai Karamcharis Act up to March 2002 and the Commission set up thereunder 
was also reconstituted. These are important steps for the benefit of the Safai 
Karamcharis. But, the position now is that the Commission today exists only in for

SHRI V.P. DURAISAMY (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Chairman, Sir, it is very 
unfortunate that the recommendations of the Eleventh Finance Commission are totally 
against the States like Tamil Nadu which are performing extremely well both on the 
economic front as well as on the social front. The Commission has punished Tamil 
Nadu and other States which have shown steady progress on the economic front and 
showed basic fiscal discipline.

recommendations is that the States which have shown economic progress are being 
deprived of their due share in the Central revenue and they have been made eligible 
for reduced share. On the other hand, the States which have squandered their resources 
and failed to effect any fiscal discipline in  their financial management are going to get 
additional share from the Central revenue. 
It is just like punishing students for securing distinction in an examination 
and giving awards to the students who have shown dismal performance.

Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Kerala and Andhra Pradesh. It is obvious that these 
States have attracted more foreign investment due to conducive atmosphere created by 
the leaders of these States which in turn contributed more to the generation of 
revenues in the country. Is it a crime to a ttract foreign investment? Is it a crime to 
show improved performance on the economic and social front? Is it not unfair to 
punish these States for attracting more investments, generating more employment, 
collecting more revenues, providing better health care, social services and managing 
resources judiciously? 
I would request the Prime Minister to convene a meeting of the Chief 
Ministers of the States which have been affected by the recommendations of the 
Eleventh Finance Commission.  Thank you.

SHRIMATI BASANTI SARMA (Assam): Sir, at the very outset, I welcome 
this Bill and congratulate Shri Suresh Pach ouri for bringing this burning subject up. It 
is of vital importance in today's time of unrest, which is prevailing in the country. 
Unemployment problem today is assuming an alarming proportion. The 
International Labour Organisations says that the number of unemployed and under-
employed in the world has never been higher and will grow by millions. According to 
the Director-General of the I.L.O., the global employment situation is grim and getting 
grimmer. Here I would like to add that we as a developing country should heed to this 
warning and wake up. 
Creation of jobs has always been at the top of the agenda of all political 
parties, but that is more of a regular exercise done to ornament the election manifesto.  
The employment situation still remains grim. 
There are currently 40 million job-seekers registered with the employment 
exchanges. The army of the unemployed is growing at different employment 
exchanges.   According to the latest data available, as
